summary: RFCs 6513, 6514 and others describe how a service provider offers Multicast VPN service to its customers, using point-to-multipoint or multipoint-to-multipoint trees in the backbone. This proposed standard describes the use of ingress replication tunnels as one type of such tree.

plainLanguage.summary: When one person must send the same message to many people, they can make one copy per person themselves. This explains that approach for private networks run by providers.

subtitle: How multicast VPN routers join, leave and label ingress replication tunnels, where the parent sends one unicast copy per child.

tldr.problem: Ingress replication was allowed as a Multicast VPN tunnel type, but unlike other types it had no setup protocol of its own, and the earlier specifications were vague about how it is identified, joined and labelled.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7988 specifies how an IR P-tunnel is identified (by route NLRI, not the PTA Tunnel Identifier), how routers join and prune with BGP Leaf A-D routes, how MPLS labels must be allocated, and which timers to use when switching parent.
tldr.outcome: It adds no new protocol elements but makes existing ones explicit, and it takes precedence over RFC 6513 and RFC 6514 where they conflict. It has been updated by RFC 10018.

facts.label: PTA fields
facts.value: Tunnel Type, MPLS Label, Tunnel Identifier, Flags

today: RFC 7988 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2016. It updates RFC 6513 and RFC 6514, and is itself updated by RFC 10018.

sections.title: Why Ingress Replication Needed Clarifying
sections.content:
RFC 6513, RFC 6514 and related RFCs describe how a service provider offers Multicast VPN (MVPN). Customer multicast traffic crosses the backbone in point-to-multipoint (P2MP) or multipoint-to-multipoint (MP2MP) tunnels called P-tunnels. One supported kind is ingress replication (IR).

Every other P-tunnel technology has its own existing setup protocol and way to name a tree. IR does not: all of its signaling is done with the BGP Auto-Discovery (A-D) routes from RFC 6514. Earlier RFCs sometimes described an IR P-tunnel as merely consisting of unicast tunnels, which hides that it is a real P2MP tree whose nodes keep multicast state in both control and data planes.

RFC 7988 adds no new protocol elements. It makes explicit how to identify, join and prune an IR P-tunnel, how to allocate MPLS labels for it, and which timers to use when switching a flow between tunnels. Because this material is needed to implement IR properly, it updates RFC 6513 and RFC 6514, and where it conflicts with them, this document takes precedence.
sections.plainLanguage: Providers already used the photocopy trick, but the rulebook was fuzzy about the details. This RFC writes the details down.

sections.title: What an IR P-tunnel Is
sections.content:
An IR P-tunnel is a P2MP tree whose nodes are BGP speakers that support MVPN procedures: usually Provider Edge (PE) routers, Autonomous System Border Routers (ASBRs) or, with RFC 7524, Area Border Routers (ABRs). A non-segmented IR P-tunnel has two levels: an ingress PE as root and the egress PEs as its children. In a segmented P-tunnel, some segments can use IR, and then the children may be ABRs or ASBRs. Each node knows its parent, also called the Upstream Multicast Hop (UMH), and its children.

What makes it distinct is how data moves from parent to child. The parent labels the packet with a P-tunnel label that the child assigned to that P-tunnel, wraps it in a unicast encapsulation and sends it through an ordinary unicast tunnel to that child. It repeats this for each child, so several copies may leave through one interface. No Layer 2 multicast, IP multicast or MPLS multicast is used.

The unicast tunnels are not specific to one IR P-tunnel. One tunnel from R1 to R2 can carry several P-tunnels and unicast traffic too, because R2 acts on the label at the top of the stack. Typically they are existing LDP or RSVP-TE LSPs. Intermediate routers keep no multicast state for the IR P-tunnel. An IR P-tunnel can instantiate either an Inclusive PMSI (I-PMSI) or a Selective PMSI (S-PMSI).
sections.plainLanguage: The sender makes one copy of the message for each receiver and sends each copy by normal mail. Each receiver put a special sticker on its own copy so it knows which group the message is for.

sections.title: How an IR P-tunnel Is Identified
sections.content:
P-tunnels are named in four BGP route types from RFC 6514: Intra-AS I-PMSI A-D, Inter-AS I-PMSI A-D, S-PMSI A-D and Leaf A-D routes. Such a route carries a PMSI Tunnel Attribute (PTA) with four fields: Tunnel Type, MPLS Label, Tunnel Identifier and Flags. For IR, Tunnel Type is set to 6.

For other tunnel types the Tunnel Identifier names the tree. For IR it does not. Instead:

  • In an S-PMSI, Intra-AS I-PMSI or Inter-AS I-PMSI A-D route, the IR P-tunnel identifier is the route's NLRI, including its Route Type and Length fields.
  • In a Leaf A-D route, the identifier is the Route Key field of the route's NLRI.

An advertising A-D route only identifies an IR P-tunnel if its PTA has Tunnel Type IR. When an IR P-tunnel is carried in an S-PMSI or Inter-AS I-PMSI A-D route, the Leaf Information Required bit MUST be set. Two routes with different NLRIs cannot advertise the same IR P-tunnel, so binding two customer flows to one IR P-tunnel needs an I-PMSI route or an S-PMSI route with wildcards.
sections.plainLanguage: The name of the group is written on the envelope the announcement came in, not in the box that usually holds names.

sections.title: Joining and Pruning
sections.content:
How a router joins depends on how the tunnel was advertised. If the advertising route has the Leaf Information Required bit set, the joiner finds its UMH (from the P2MP Segmented Next Hop Extended Community if present, otherwise from the route's next hop) and originates a Leaf A-D route. The UMH MUST be identified by an IP-address-specific Route Target on that route. The PTA has Tunnel Type IR, a Tunnel Identifier as described in Section 5, and a non-zero MPLS Label, the P-tunnel label.

If the bit is not set (only possible for Intra-AS I-PMSI A-D routes), the set of IR P-tunnels is joined all at once by originating an Intra-AS I-PMSI A-D route with a non-zero MPLS label, which must bind one to one to the I-PMSI. Unadvertised IR P-tunnels can be joined only with the global table multicast procedures of RFC 7524.

To prune, a router withdraws the route it used to join. To keep the tunnel through a different parent, it changes the Route Target of its Leaf A-D route. A parent treats a changed Route Target that no longer names it exactly like a withdrawal. A parent also must handle a Leaf A-D route that arrives before the matching S-PMSI A-D route, since events may not occur in the usual order.
sections.plainLanguage: To join the group you send a note saying which sender you want copies from and which sticker to use. To leave, you take the note back.

sections.title: Tunnel Identifier, Labels and Wrong-PE Discards
sections.content:
For an IR PTA, the Tunnel Identifier is significant only in a Leaf A-D route or when the Leaf Information Required bit is not set. Then it holds a routable IP address of the route originator, which the UMH uses to pick the unicast tunnel toward it. Otherwise it MUST be ignored. Even when ignored, it should be an IP address, and the RFC recommends a routable address of the router that built the PTA. The MPLS Label field is significant under the same two conditions; otherwise it SHOULD be zero when sent and MUST be ignored on receipt.

Egress PEs infer the ingress PE from the P-tunnel label to apply the Discarding Packets from the Wrong PE procedure of RFC 6513. The label of two IR P-tunnels with different roots MUST NOT be the same. When an egress node changes the Route Target of a Leaf A-D route it MUST also change the label, so packets from the old and new parent can be told apart. To support the extranet procedures of RFC 7900, labels MUST be unique for the triple of root, root RD and parent node. Intermediate nodes need distinct non-zero labels for different route keys unless the parent, downstream neighbours and encapsulation are all identical.

The IP source address of the encapsulating header is not used to find the ingress PE, for several stated reasons, such as segmented tunnels and extranet needing the ingress VRF. If a PE joined using the Intra-AS I-PMSI method, it cannot infer the ingress PE this way, so duplicate prevention needs Single Forwarder Selection or native PIM procedures.
sections.plainLanguage: The sticker on each copy tells the receiver where it came from, so it can throw away duplicate copies. If the receiver switches senders, it uses a new sticker.

sections.title: Timers When Switching Parent
sections.content:
A child switches its UMH by changing the Route Target and the PTA label of its Leaf A-D route in one control-plane operation. The NLRI is not modified. That single operation both joins the new parent and prunes the old one, so make-before-break is not possible directly.

Two timers fix this. The old UMH MUST keep transmitting for a while after it sees the Leaf A-D route withdrawn or its Route Target changed: the parent-continues timer, which SHOULD default to 60 seconds and be configurable. The child MUST run a switch-parents-delay timer after changing the Route Target, which SHOULD default to 30 seconds and be configurable. Until it expires the child keeps accepting packets from the old UMH, though it MAY treat the timer as expired once a packet arrives from the new UMH. The parent-continues timer MUST be longer than the switch-parents-delay timer, and both are specific to one IR P-tunnel.
sections.plainLanguage: When you change who sends you copies, the old sender keeps sending a little longer and you keep listening to both for a short time, so you do not miss anything.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: RFC 7988 raises no security considerations beyond those already discussed in RFC 6513 and RFC 6514.
sections.plainLanguage: This clarification does not add any new risks beyond those the older rules already had.
